Heimersheim and Nanda distinguish denoising patches (clean activations into a corrupted run: evidence of sufficiency for restoration in that context) from noising patches (corrupted activations into a clean run: evidence concerning necessity). Neither establishes a complete mechanism: redundancy can hide contributions, and interacting components may require joint patches. Intermediate component and path interventions help test where information acts and how components interact. These conclusions depend on the chosen inputs, intervention and metric. [How to use and interpret activation patching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15255)

Applied to a causal residual convolution recommender, a direct mathematical consequence is that replacing the entire final scoring representation with its clean value restores clean scores whenever the unchanged deterministic scorer depends only on that representation and fixed item embeddings. This is a useful implementation control, but supplies no localization of the upstream computation. More informative experiments patch intermediate convolution branches, positions or paths, then recompute downstream layers; compare both patch directions and targeted controls. Even naturally occurring donor activations can create unfamiliar hybrid states when combined with recipient activations. Zhang and Nanda demonstrate sensitivity to corruption methods and metrics, including evidence of distribution artifacts from Gaussian corruption; they recommend semantically matched input replacements and logit differences. For recommendation, candidate-score margins provide an analogous continuous diagnostic, alongside ranking outcomes. The recommender-specific conclusions here are deductions, not experiments reported in these papers. [Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042)
